blocks.text: In flight itself the flock has the form of a triangle, which, driven at its base by the winds, cuts the air with its apex. Cicero, book 2 On the Nature of the Gods: "This too was observed by Aristotle: that cranes, when they cross the seas seeking warmer regions, form the shape of a triangle. With its apex the air in front of them is pushed aside. Then gradually, on either side, the course of the birds is borne up by their wings as by oars. And the base of the triangle which the cranes form is helped by the winds, as if from the stern." Plutarch, in the book Whether Land or Sea Animals, etc.: Εἰς τρίγωνον συνάγουσαι σχίζουσι τῇ κορυφῇ τὸ πνεῦμα περιῤῥέον, ὥστε μὴ διασπᾶσθαι τὴν τάξιν· [Eis trigōnon synagousai schizousi tē koryphē to pneuma perirrheon, hōste mē diaspasthai tēn taxin] "Gathered into a triangle, they cut with its apex the wind flowing around them, so that their line is not broken up." Aelian, book 13, ch. 13: Τρίγωνον ὀξύγονον τὸ σχῆμα τῆς πτήσεως ἀποφαίνουσι, ἵνα ἐμπίπτουσαι τῷ ἀέρι διακόπτωσιν αὐτόν· [Trigōnon oxygonon to schēma tēs ptēseōs apophainousi, hina empiptousai tō aeri diakoptōsin auton] "They shape their flight into an acute-angled triangle, so that, striking into the air, they may cut it more easily." Philes also asserts that they fly
Εἰς ὀρμαθὸν τρίστοιχον ὀξυγωνίου, [Eis hormathon tristoichon oxygōniou]
"in a three-sided formation with acute angles." And Tzetzes:
Τρίγωνον ὀξυγώνιον ποιοῦνται τούτων πτῆσιν, [Trigōnon oxygōnion poiountai toutōn ptēsin] ^{a)} [col. 74] Ὡς τὸν ἀέρα τέμνωσιν οὕτως εὐμαρεστέρως, [Hōs ton aera temnōsin houtōs eumaresterōs]

"They make their flight an acute-angled triangle, so that they may thus divide the air more easily." Indeed, by this triangular figure they are thought to imitate certain letters, namely A, V, Δ, Λ, Υ. Hence Jerome, Epist. 4 to Rusticus: "Cranes follow one leader in a lettered order." So too Isidore. This sheds light on these lines of Lucan on cranes, book 5, line 712:

— — — and in their first flight they form various figures, as chance directs; soon, when Notus strikes their outstretched wings from higher up, [II, 623] they are heedlessly mingled and massed into confused circles, and the letter, thrown into disorder, perishes as their feathers scatter.
You will throw the lines into disorder, and the letter will not fly whole, if you lose a single bird of Palamedes.
And on the name of Earinus, book 9, Epigram 14:
Which cranes, with writing wing, raise to the stars.
I am a letter of the sky, written out by a flying wing.
I would prefer perscripta volante [written out by (me) flying]. And Claudian, in The Gildonic War, where he speaks of cranes:
In varied ranks a huge letter is woven across the clouds, and the air is inscribed with the marks of their wings.

And Cassiodorus, Variae book 8, Epistle 12: "For even today cranes, which form a fleet together, trace the shapes of the alphabet, nature instructing them." And in Philostratus' Heroicus, Ulysses, seeing cranes flying in their usual manner, looked at Palamedes and said: Αἱ γέρανοι, ἔφη, μαρτύρονται τοὺς Ἀχαιοὺς, ὅτι αὗται γράμματα εὗρον, οὐχὶ σύ· [Hai geranoi, ephē, martyrontai tous Achaious, hoti hautai grammata heuron, ouchi sy] "The cranes," he said, "testify to the Greeks that they, not you, invented letters." I would read τοῖς Ἀχαιοῖς [tois Achaiois], not τοὺς Ἀχαιούς [tous Achaious]. And Nazianzen, Oration 34: Τίνος Παλαμήδους τακτικὰ, κινήματά τε, καὶ σχήματα γεράνων, ὡς πᾶσι, καὶ ταῦτα παιδεύματα, κινουμένων ἐν τάξει, καὶ μετὰ ποικίλης τῆς πτήσεως; [Tinos Palamēdous taktika, kinēmata te, kai schēmata geranōn, hōs pasi, kai tauta paideumata, kinoumenōn en taxei, kai meta poikilēs tēs ptēseōs] "Of what Palamedes are the ordered movements, figures and precepts of the cranes, by which, as they say, they move in battle line with varied flight?" The same birds, when an eagle is sighted, ^{b)} κολπωσάμεναι, μηνοειδὲς τὸ μέσον ἀποφήνασαι, ἀπειλοῦσιν ὡς ἀντιταξόμεναι, [kolpōsamenai, mēnoeides to meson apophēnasai, apeilousin hōs antitaxomenai] "opening a hollow so that they imitate the appearance of the crescent moon, threaten as if about to resist"; and the eagle retreats and checks its flight.
